summary: Jon Postel suggests using eight-character standard host names and gives a list pairing network site numbers with standard and alternate names. It is part of a debate on how to name hosts. It was replaced by RFC 236.

eli5.summary: A suggestion for a list of eight-letter nicknames for each computer on the network. It was one of several competing lists.

subtitle: A proposed standard for eight-character host names on the ARPA Network.

tldr.problem: As the ARPA Network grew, there was no agreed standard for naming hosts. Different sites and communities used different naming conventions, making it difficult to remember and refer to network hosts consistently.
tldr.mechanism: Jon Postel proposes using eight-character names for all ARPA Network hosts and provides a list pairing each known network site number with a standard name (such as UCLA-NMC, SRI-ARC, BBN-NCC) and sometimes an alternate short name.
tldr.outcome: The proposal was one of several competing naming schemes in circulation at the time and was superseded by other naming conventions, but it reflects early thinking about standardization.

today: RFC 229 was quickly superseded by RFC 236, another Standard Host Names proposal. Neither became the standard in use; eventually, the Domain Name System (DNS) provided a hierarchical, globally scalable approach to host naming that replaced these early flat-list schemes.

sections.title: The Need for Standard Host Names
sections.content:
By September 1971, the ARPA Network included dozens of host computers at research institutions, government sites, and contractors. Each site had its own local name or identifier, but there was no agreed-upon standard for referring to them across the network. Users and programmers had to remember and use different names depending on context and communication method.

Jon Postel, of the UCLA Network Measurement Center, proposes a standard eight-character host naming scheme. Eight characters was a practical length—short enough to type easily on typewriter-based terminals, yet long enough to be mnemonic and descriptive.
sections.eli5: Different places called their computers different names, making it confusing. Postel suggested a standard list of nicknames so everyone would use the same names.

sections.title: The Proposed Names
sections.content:
Postel's list pairs each network site number with a standard name and sometimes an alternate (shorter) name. For example, UCLA's Network Measurement Center is UCLA-NMC (alternate: SEX, presumably an acronym). Stanford Research Institute is SRI-ARC (alternate: NIC). BBN has multiple sites: BBN-NCC, BBN-A, and BBN-B. Other sites include MIT, RAND, UCSB, the University of Utah, and MIT's Multics system.

The names are geographically or organizationally descriptive, making them easier to remember than bare numbers. The list documents site numbers ranging from 1 to 158, showing the scope of the early ARPA Network.
sections.eli5: You could look up a site's number and see what name to use for it, like UCLA-NMC for site 1, or SRI-ARC for site 2.

sections.title: One of Several Competing Proposals
sections.content: The RFC notes that this proposal is related to RFC 226 (another naming proposal) and mentions debates about how to standardize host identification. RFC 236 (Standard Host Names) superseded this RFC, suggesting that the naming question remained unsettled even as standardization efforts continued. Eventually, the Domain Name System (DNS) and later internet naming conventions would replace these early ad-hoc schemes.
sections.eli5: This was just one idea among several about how to name computers. People didn't agree on a single standard right away.

references.text: Kalin, M. D., "Standardization of Host Mnemonics", RFC 226, September 1971.
Postel, J. B., "Standard Host Names", RFC 236, September 1971.
